name: Karashi mentaiko (Hakata spicy pollock roe)
text: Salted, chili-seasoned walleye pollock roe, the signature food of Hakata. Fukuya founder Kawahara Toshio (shop founded 5 Oct 1948 after repatriation from Manchuria) put it on sale on 10 Jan 1949. Sources trace the prototype to the Korean salted roe preparation (myeongran-jeot) he had eaten in Busan. Roe was sourced from Hokkaido pollock because the fish is not caught off Fukuoka.
flavor: Salty-savory roe with chili heat and a seasoned-liquor depth; the Hakata style is adjusted milder and rounder for Japanese palates than the Korean original.
use: Eaten as is over rice, as a sake accompaniment, grilled lightly, or folded into pasta, rice balls and sauces. Distinct from plain tarako, which is the unseasoned salted roe.
craft: Sources say Kawahara needed roughly ten years of trials, with 'Aji no Mentaiko' released in 1957 (one casual source says c. 1954; treat as unreliable). He took out no patent and taught the method to anyone who asked, which is why Hakata has many competing makers. One source claims Shimonoseki as the origin, a minority view. When judging, check skin integrity, roe grain, even colour and how the heat sits against the salt.

name: Game-ni (Fukuoka stewed chicken and root vegetables)
text: Fukuoka's celebration and New Year stew of chicken and root vegetables, sautéed in oil then simmered in dashi and seasonings. It is nearly the same as the nationally known chikuzen-ni, though game-ni is described as having larger pieces and sometimes bone-in chicken. The name is explained either from the Hakata dialect 'game-kurikomu' (to gather up) or from a Bunroku-era story of soldiers simmering suppon (soft-shelled turtle) with vegetables; sources call both theories.
flavor: Sweet-savory, oil-rounded simmered flavour with distinct, separately cooked vegetable textures.
use: Served at New Year and festive occasions, and also as a shojin (temple) dish; today chicken has replaced suppon.
craft: Sources describe the basic sequence: stir-fry chicken and roots in oil first, then add dashi and seasoning and simmer. The oil-first step and the cut size are what separate it from a plain nimono. Cut vegetables large and uniform so they hold shape through the simmer.

name: Goma-saba (Hakata sesame mackerel)
text: Raw mackerel fillet slices dressed in a sesame-soy sauce, a Hakata regional dish also eaten over rice or as an ochazuke. An RKB broadcast piece on its history suggests it may date from the late Edo to early Meiji period, when soy sauce became widely available. The earliest printed appearance found was in a 1984 (Showa 59) regional cookbook, as 'saba no goma-shoyu'.
flavor: Rich, nutty sesame and sweet soy over the oily, clean flesh of fresh mackerel.
use: Served as an appetizer or sake dish, or with rice and hot tea poured over it.
craft: Because it is raw mackerel, freshness decides everything; the sauce is there to complement the fish's fat, not hide it. The age of the dish is uncertain: the Edo–Meiji origin is a hypothesis, and the written record found only goes back to 1984.
src: RKB: the history of Hakata goma-saba

name: Yobuko ika ikizukuri (live squid sashimi)
text: Squid served as sashimi while still alive, the signature of Yobuko on the Genkai Sea coast (Karatsu). Spear squid (yari-ika), swordtip squid (kensaki-ika) and bigfin reef squid (aori-ika) are used. The preparation is said to take only some tens of seconds. The restaurant Kawataro, said to be Japan's first ikesu (live-tank) restaurant, opened in 1961 (Showa 36). It is listed in the MAFF 100 regional dishes.
flavor: Translucent, crisp then sticky flesh with sweetness; the legs are often fried or simmered afterward.
use: Sashimi in a tank-to-table service, followed by the trimmings as tempura or in soup.
craft: The skill is speed and clean cutting from a live squid, so that the flesh stays translucent and the tentacles still move. Species and season change the texture: the sources name three species but do not rank them.
src: Premium Outlets Times: Saga B-grade foods

name: Sicilian rice (Saga)
text: Saga city's local plate: warm rice topped with raw vegetables and sweet-salty stir-fried meat and onion, finished with mayonnaise. It began around 1975 (Showa 50) as a staff meal at an eatery and then spread through kissaten (coffee-shop) menus. The origin of the name is not settled, and the sources list several theories without confirming one.
flavor: Sweet-salty meat sauce against cold crisp vegetables, with the cream of mayonnaise tying them together.
use: A kissaten and diner lunch plate, eaten with a spoon or fork.
craft: The contrast of hot rice and meat against raw vegetables is the point; a professional keeps the vegetables cold and cut fine and seasons the meat firmly enough to flavour the rice beneath. Beef or pork variations are found; the sources do not fix a standard.

name: Suko-zushi (Shiraishi)
text: A sushi of Shiraishi town, Kishima district, using produce of the Ariake Sea and the mountains. Tradition says that about 500 years ago (Muromachi period) the townspeople, grateful for their lord's kindness, made it as an offering. The sources present this as tradition and not documented history.
flavor: Mild, layered pressed-sushi taste from sea and mountain ingredients.
use: A festive and ceremonial regional sushi.
craft: The legend is the only dating the sources give; I did not find figures for the rice, vinegar or layering order in the results, so confirm the recipe with local makers.
src: Agency for Cultural Affairs: 100-year foods, Saga

name: Turkish rice (Nagasaki)
text: A Nagasaki yoshoku one-plate meal of pilaf (or fried rice), spaghetti (Neapolitan) and pork cutlet, usually with demi-glace. Its date is usually put in the 1950s but no firm record was found. The name is unexplained: the best-known theory is that the three colours suggested the tricolore, which became 'Turko'; others cite a Meiji-period 'Turkish rice' in the Jiji Shimpo, or a Kobe naval officers' club cook adapting pilaf from cold rice.
flavor: Hearty and sweet-savory; crisp cutlet, tomato spaghetti and buttery rice in one dish.
use: A cafe and diner main, served all in one plate.
craft: Components vary (pilaf vs fried rice, Neapolitan vs other pasta, sauce) so there is no single standard. A professional balances fat and acidity across the three parts and keeps the cutlet crisp under the sauce.
src: macaroni: Nagasaki Turkish rice, origin and recipe

name: Nagasaki kakuni-manju (braised pork belly bun)
text: A steamed bun filled with soy-braised pork belly. The roots lie in the tonpo-rou (Dongpo pork) of Nagasaki's shippoku banquet cooking, a Chinese-derived dish. Iwasaki Honpo, founded in 1965 (Showa 40), is credited with marketing it as 'Nagasaki kakuni-manju' under first-generation Iwasaki Hirotaka, who wanted a handier, tastier tonpo-rou.
flavor: Melting fat and sweet-savory soy braise in a soft, fluffy bun.
use: Eaten out of hand as a street snack or souvenir.
craft: Sources differ on origin: one account (citing a Nagasaki City article) says the braised pork and bun dough were originally served separately in Chinese courses, and guests made their own sandwich. The braise should be soft enough to melt but hold its cube; the bun must be fluffy rather than dense.

name: Taipien (Kumamoto glass-noodle soup)
text: A Kumamoto noodle soup of harusame (glass noodles) with fried egg, vegetables and seafood, introduced by Fujian overseas Chinese. Sources say it came from Fujian to Nagasaki and Kumamoto in the late Meiji period, though origins are described as uncertain. Kumamoto developed its own version.
flavor: Light, clean, deep broth with the richness of the fried egg and the slippery harusame.
use: Eaten as a noodle meal; seen as a lighter alternative to wheat noodles.
craft: Kumamoto's version centres on the fried egg and glass noodles. The sources give no fixed broth recipe; judge the broth clarity and how well the harusame keeps its texture.

name: Dago-jiru (Kumamoto dumpling soup)
text: A Kumamoto soup in which 'dago' (dialect for dumpling) are flattened pieces of kneaded wheat-flour dough simmered with seasonal vegetables such as hakusai, daikon and carrot and sometimes meat, seasoned with miso or soy sauce. It is said to have arisen so that farmers could eat quickly between jobs. Ingredients and seasoning vary by area.
flavor: Homey, filling soup with soft, chewy dumplings.
use: A staple home dish and a regional restaurant dish.
craft: Dough is rested and stretched thin by hand; miso or soy seasoning is regional, so there is no single standard. Add dumplings only when the broth is boiling.

name: Dango-jiru (Oita)
text: An Oita miso soup with thin, hand-stretched, noodle-like wheat dumplings, together with taro, shiitake and burdock. MAFF's regional-cooking database lists it for Oita. Plateau terrain with little rice land favoured wheat and other grains, giving the region a flour-eating culture.
flavor: Hearty miso soup with chewy, thin dumplings and earthy root vegetables.
use: A cold-season home dish and local restaurant staple.
craft: The dough is stretched by hand into thin strips; thinness is the quality marker. Compare with Kumamoto's dago-jiru, which uses flatter pieces and varied seasoning.

name: Tori-ten (Oita chicken tempura)
text: Marinated chicken coated in tempura batter and deep-fried, eaten with vinegar-soy and karashi mustard. It is credited to an Oita City shokudo in 1962 (Showa 37), but the sources note multiple theories and that it has been eaten across Oita since the Showa era.
flavor: Soft, juicy chicken in a light batter, with sharp vinegar-soy and mustard heat.
use: A shokudo and izakaya staple, also a lunch set.
craft: Seasoned before battering (unlike plain tempura) and eaten with karashi and ponzu-style sauce. Unlike karaage, the coating is tempura batter; check that it is light and crisp, with juicy flesh.

name: Ryukyu (Oita marinated fish rice bowl)
text: Fresh fish slices marinated in a soy-based sauce, placed on rice with condiments. Described as a fisherman's meal and a preservation method, it is said to have spread from the southern coast of Oita to the whole prefecture. Kabosu is a common accent.
flavor: Salty-sweet soy-marinated raw fish over warm rice, with kabosu citrus brightness.
use: Eaten as a rice bowl or as a sake appetiser.
craft: Marinating time sets texture; sources do not give a ratio or time, so judge by the fish: leaner fish tolerate longer soaking. Sauces typically also contain sesame or ginger; sources do not specify.

name: Seki-aji and seki-saba (Saganoseki)
text: Brand horse mackerel and chub mackerel caught by single-line (ippon-zuri) fishing off Saganoseki in eastern Oita. They are served as sashimi and also made into ichiya-boshi (overnight dried) and fry.
flavor: Firm, sweet, fat-balanced flesh when fresh.
use: Premium sashimi in Oita, with processed forms.
craft: The brand rests on the line-caught method and place; line-caught fish suffer less damage than netted fish. The sources here do not give grading or handling specifics.
src: Mapple: where to eat Seki-aji and Seki-saba

name: Hiya-jiru (Miyazaki cold soup)
text: A summer home dish of the Miyazaki plain, poured cold over barley rice. MAFF describes it as an instant poured soup. Iriko (dried small fish) and miso are grilled, thinned with dashi, and finished with shiso, cucumber and tofu.
flavor: Cool, toasted-miso and dried-fish savour, with the freshness of shiso and cucumber.
use: Eaten in hot weather over cold barley rice or rice.
craft: Grilling the miso and iriko gives the aroma that distinguishes it from a plain cold miso soup. Serve the soup well chilled and add the garnish just before serving.

name: Keihan (Amami chicken rice)
text: A dish of Amami: shredded chicken, dried shiitake and shredded egg over rice, with chicken-bone broth poured over. The Kagoshima prefectural food-culture page says Amami people served it to Satsuma officials in the Edo period, and that it was chosen as one of MAFF's 100 rural regional dishes in 2007.
flavor: Clean, savoury chicken broth with the contrasts of egg, mushroom and shredded chicken.
use: A bowl eaten like ochazuke, with toppings added at the table.
craft: Broth clarity and depth are the judging points; toppings are cut fine and kept separate. The sources give no stock recipe details.

name: Satsuma-jiru
text: A miso soup rich with chicken and vegetables. MAFF says it is said to have begun when Satsuma samurai killed the defeated cocks of cockfights and simmered them with vegetables. It was once a celebratory dish and is now eaten especially in winter.
flavor: Rich chicken and vegetable miso soup.
use: A winter home dish and festive soup.
craft: Chicken provides the stock; vegetables are cut generously. Compare with the pork-based tonjiru.

name: Kibinago kibi-sashi
text: Kibinago, a small herring-family fish called 'tears of the Kuroshio' in the Kagoshima prefectural page. The standard form is kibi-sashi: hand-opened and eaten with vinegared miso.
flavor: Delicate, lightly fatty small fish with sharp vinegared-miso.
use: A sashimi and sake appetiser in Kagoshima.
craft: The fish is opened by hand; sources do not give a detailed method, but freshness and clean fillets are the points to check.

name: Shirokuma (Kagoshima shaved ice)
text: Kagoshima's shaved ice with condensed milk, fruit and amanatto (sweet beans). The prefectural page lists several theories for the name: a polar bear picture on the condensed-milk tin, or the top-down shape resembling a polar bear face.
flavor: Milky sweetness with fruit and sweet beans.
use: A summer dessert.
craft: Sources do not specify exact toppings or ice texture, only the components. The name theories are unverified.

name: Soki-jiru (Okinawan pork spare-rib soup)
text: A soup of pork spare ribs (soki) simmered until the meat falls from the bone, with daikon in winter or winter melon in summer. In sources, the pork goes into cold water, is skimmed, then kombu and dried shiitake are added and the soup is simmered on low heat about 1.5 hours.
flavor: Pork-rich, clean soup with soft meat.
use: Served as a main in a bowl at Okinawan shokudo and at home.
craft: Start from cold water and skim carefully; low heat for around 1.5 hours is the figure in one source. Seasonal choice of daikon or winter melon is traditional.

name: Jimami-tofu (Okinawan peanut tofu)
text: A tofu-like set made from pressed peanut milk ('jimami' is the Okinawan word for peanut) with sweet potato starch. It contains no soybeans and no nigari. The texture is chewy, and it is served with a sweet sauce.
flavor: Soft, springy and chewy, with a peanut richness and light sweetness.
use: A small side dish at the start or end of a meal.
craft: Starch gelation sets it, not coagulant. Sources do not give ratios; the check is a smooth, chewy set with a clean peanut flavour.

name: Taco rice (Kin town)
text: Taco filling served over rice. Sources describe it as a recent creation, from the 1980s, with Kin town and the restaurant King Tacos as the best-known origin. Accounts that it was made for US military personnel appear but are only one version.
flavor: Spiced minced meat, cheese and fresh vegetables over rice.
use: A casual Okinawan lunch and take-away meal.
craft: The sources give little technique. The comparison is to Mexican tacos, with rice instead of tortilla.

name: Nakami-jiru (Okinawan offal soup)
text: A clear soup of pork offal ('nakami'). Cleaning is crucial: the offal is rubbed with flour or salt and boiled repeatedly to remove odour. The base is usually katsuobushi dashi. It has been served at celebrations and for guests.
flavor: Clean, mild soup with soft offal.
use: A festive and formal soup in Okinawa.
craft: The preparation (rubbing with flour and salt, repeated blanching) is the whole skill. A cloudy or smelly result means incomplete cleaning.

name: Ikasumi-jiru (Okinawan squid ink soup)
text: A soup of white squid and pork simmered in katsuobushi and kombu dashi, finished with squid ink and salt. In Okinawa it has long been treated as kusuimun (medicinal food).
flavor: Black, briny, rich seafood-and-pork soup.
use: A traditional soup in Okinawan cooking.
craft: Ink goes in at the end so the flavour stays fresh; season with salt only. Sources give no more detail.

name: Tofuyo (Okinawan fermented tofu)
text: Tofu slowly fermented with rice koji, red koji and awamori. It is vivid red, salty and rich.
flavor: Salty, cheese-like richness with a red-koji and awamori aroma.
use: Eaten in small pieces as a sake accompaniment.
craft: The results did not give the process in detail; the three fermenting agents are koji, red koji and awamori.
